mcqs.question: Why does `n & (n - 1)` turn off exactly the lowest set bit of n and leave every other bit unchanged?
options: Subtracting 1 borrows from the lowest set bit, flipping it to 0 and flipping every bit below it to 1, so ANDing recombines everything except that one bit into zero below it and unchanged above it
Subtraction in binary always clears the most significant bit first
AND between any two consecutive integers always produces zero
n - 1 reverses the bit order of n, so ANDing cancels the lowest bit by symmetry
mcqs.explanation: The borrow from subtracting 1 ripples exactly up to the lowest set bit: that bit flips off, everything below it flips on, and everything above is untouched — ANDing the two patterns keeps the unchanged upper bits, zeroes the flipped bit, and zeroes the now-opposite lower bits. It has nothing to do with bit-order reversal or most-significant bits, and AND of consecutive integers is not generally zero (e.g. 6 & 5 = 4).

mcqs.question: For an integer with only 3 bits set, out of 64 total bits, how many iterations does Brian Kernighan's popcount loop run compared to the naive shift-and-check loop?
options: 3 iterations for Kernighan's loop versus 64 for the naive loop
64 iterations for both, since both must inspect every bit position
3 iterations for the naive loop versus 64 for Kernighan's loop
log2(64) = 6 iterations for Kernighan's loop versus 64 for the naive loop
mcqs.explanation: Kernighan's loop clears one set bit per iteration and stops when n reaches zero, so it costs exactly one iteration per set bit — 3 here — regardless of the integer's width. The naive loop shifts and checks every bit position once, so it always costs the full width, 64, no matter how sparse the number is.

mcqs.question: What does `n & -n` compute, and how does that differ from `n & (n - 1)`?
options: n & -n isolates the lowest set bit as a standalone value; n & (n-1) clears that same bit instead
They compute the same value; -n and n-1 are equivalent bit patterns in two's complement
n & -n counts the total number of set bits in n directly
n & -n clears the highest set bit, while n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit
mcqs.explanation: In two's complement, -n matches n below the lowest set bit and is n's complement above it, so ANDing keeps only that one position — isolating rather than removing it. n & (n-1) does the opposite operation, clearing that bit. -n and n-1 are different bit patterns (e.g. for n=6, -6 is ...11111010 while 5 is ...00000101), and neither expression counts bits by itself.

mcqs.question: Why does the power-of-two check need an explicit `n > 0` guard alongside `(n & (n - 1)) == 0`?
options: Without it, negative numbers under two's complement always evaluate to true
Without it, n = 0 satisfies (n & (n-1)) == 0 and would be incorrectly reported as a power of two
The guard is only a style convention and has no effect on correctness
Without it, the expression throws a division-by-zero error at n = 0
mcqs.explanation: At n = 0 there's no set bit to clear, so the AND is trivially 0 even though zero is not a power of two — the guard is what excludes that case. Negative numbers don't uniformly pass the check (most fail it since they have many set bits under two's complement), and there's no division involved, so no such error can occur.

mcqs.question: In production code where a fast bit count matters, which approach is generally preferred over Brian Kernighan's loop, and why?
options: A precomputed lookup table, because it is always faster than any built-in function
The naive shift-and-check loop, because it has predictable timing regardless of input
A built-in popcount function, because it typically compiles to a single hardware instruction and beats a hand-rolled loop on both speed and correctness risk
Brian Kernighan's loop itself, because no language exposes a faster alternative
mcqs.explanation: Most languages expose a built-in that compiles down to a single POPCNT-style instruction, which is faster than any loop-based approach and removes a place to introduce bugs. A lookup table can be competitive but isn't universally faster than a hardware instruction, and built-ins do exist in essentially every mainstream language, so Kernighan's loop is not the production default.

mcqs.question: A candidate writes `is_power_of_two(n) = (n & (n - 1)) == 0` with no other guard. What is the concrete bug?
options: is_power_of_two(0) returns True, incorrectly classifying zero as a power of two
is_power_of_two(1) returns False, incorrectly rejecting the smallest power of two
The function throws an exception whenever n is negative
The function is correct as written and needs no additional guard
mcqs.explanation: At n = 0 there is no set bit to clear, so the AND evaluates to 0 and the unguarded function reports zero as a power of two, which is wrong. n = 1 works correctly (1 & 0 == 0, correctly true), and the expression doesn't raise on negative inputs — it just doesn't reliably identify them as non-powers-of-two either way, which is why the guard is needed.
